decision_title: SPEC 6 projects a node with metadata to a wrapper object, not sibling keys
decision_reason: Sibling keys ("<key>$confidence") cannot express metadata on an array element -- SPEC 5 makes an array element a node, but a sibling needs a parent key to hang from. They also collide: a literal t$confidence key clashes with the projection of 't: 1 ~0.5', and the collision is manufactured by the projection so SPEC 3's duplicate-key rule never sees it. And SPEC 6 contradicted itself -- it claimed the projection was reconstructable while the shape the corpus enforced discarded confidence and annotations entirely. The wrapper is keyed on the NODE, so object values and array elements behave identically, $-prefixed keys are reserved so nothing collides, and it round-trips. It also matches the precedent $synthesize already set: a distinguishing object, never a bare value.
summary: Decision: SPEC 6 projects a node with metadata to a wrapper object, not sibling keys

rejected_alternatives.option: keep value-only and drop SPEC 6's round-trip claim

outcome: Only 2 of 8 existing valid vectors changed; grammar untouched so format stays 1.0. Rust 13/13, Python 16/16.

decision_title: Settle the SPEC 6 gap BEFORE writing more language implementations
decision_reason: Every new parser inherits an ambiguous contract. Fixing it at two implementations (Rust + Python) is far cheaper than at four. Vindicated immediately: the new conformance vectors exposed two real bugs in the Rust reference that had been invisible because the old projection discarded the evidence.
summary: Decision: Settle the SPEC 6 gap BEFORE writing more language implementations
outcome: Found: @cson attaching to the following node instead of setting document version; array elements dropping trailing annotations.

decision_title: Language implementations live in impl/<lang>/ in this repo, not separate repos
decision_reason: The conformance corpus is the contract (SPEC 8). Keeping parsers beside it means tests reference vectors by relative path and one checkout can run every implementation, so a parser cannot silently drift from the corpus. SPEC's 'cson-py' phrasing hints at separate repos; that remains reversible -- the layout moves cleanly.
summary: Decision: Language implementations live in impl/<lang>/ in this repo, not separate repos
Absent confidence is NOT 1.0 (SPEC 4.2). Absent means 'no claim'; every parser must keep the two distinguishable, including in the JSON projection.

The conformance corpus is the contract (SPEC 8). A parser is conforming iff it passes every vector; a grammar or projection change means updating the corpus and EVERY implementation in the same commit.
Keys beginning with '$' are reserved in a projected object, so a document key can never collide with a wrapper member ($value / $confidence / $annotations / $synthesize).

A conformance corpus can fail to constrain the thing it looks like it constrains. Before this session the corpus dropped confidence from its projection, so a parser collapsing absent-confidence to 1.0 passed EVERY vector while violating SPEC 4.2. Fixed by the confidence_absent_vs_one vector -- but the general lesson stands: when adding a spec rule, add a vector that FAILS without it.

The JSON projection lived only in tests/conformance.rs, not in the library -- so the corpus was testing a shape no caller could reach, and CsonDocument::to_json() (serde struct form) was something else again. Three shapes in one repo. Projection now lives in src/project.rs and the harness calls it.

@cson is document metadata (SPEC 2.5), not an annotation on the following node. The Rust parser pushed it onto pending_annotations unconditionally; invisible until the projection stopped discarding annotations.

An array element is a NODE (SPEC 5), so it may carry confidence and annotations. The Rust array loop hardcoded 'annotations: vec![]', leaving a trailing @note unconsumed for the next iteration to misparse as a value.

Validate a parser against a real document, not just the corpus. The 13 toy vectors did not exercise content-addressed keys, stacked annotations, @corpus(1.0) args or long escaped strings; a 156MB production corpus did, at ~10MB/s.

Format v1.0 draft, grammar stable. SPEC 6 projection settled on the wrapper rule (381bad3). Two parsers -- Rust reference (src/) and Python (impl/python/) -- both pass the full corpus and produce identical projections. Corpus: 11 valid + 5 invalid vectors.

SPEC 6 settled on a single wrapper rule and the first non-Rust parser landed. The new vectors immediately exposed two real bugs in the Rust reference (@cson attaching to the next node; array elements dropping annotations), both now fixed. Projection moved out of the test harness into src/project.rs.
next: Parsers for JavaScript/TypeScript then Go, built against the settled contract. A CSON printer (parse-only today). Close from_json round-trip against the wrapper projection. Read SPEC.md then conformance/README.md before changing anything -- the corpus is the contract, and a parser must never diverge from it.

summary: crush-notebook reimplements CSON's annotation concept in JSON instead of using it. Its agent-native model (docs/AGENT-NATIVE.md) is built on @wip/@temporary/@decision annotations with properties (@wip.started_by), but .crush-nb is plain JSON with a JSON Schema and crush-notebook-core depends only on serde/serde_json/uuid/thiserror -- no cson anywhere in the repo. crush-ast by contrast IS correctly on crush-cson (crush-index flattens semantic keys as (intent, file, confidence) next to decisions and the dejavue timeline). Captain 2026-09-20: both crush-ast and crush-notebook should use cson; revisit later.

Cross-language projection comparison must NORMALISE numbers. SPEC 2.3 makes every number an IEEE-754 double, but languages render them differently -- Python emits 8080.0, JavaScript emits 8080. A naive string diff of the two projections reported 6 of 11 vectors as divergent when the values were identical. impl/js/test/cross-check.mjs normalises before comparing; CSON-10's CI must do the same.

decision_title: Every implementation must be cross-checked against the others, not only against its own expectations
decision_reason: SPEC 8 promises that parsers do not diverge from the corpus. 'Each implementation passes its own tests' is a weaker claim than 'all implementations agree' -- two parsers can each be self-consistent and still disagree. At three implementations this stops being checkable by hand, so impl/js/test/cross-check.mjs asserts Rust, Python and JavaScript project identically for every vector.
summary: Decision: Every implementation must be cross-checked against the others, not only against its own expectations

Format v1.0 draft, grammar stable, SPEC 6 settled (wrapper rule). THREE implementations -- Rust reference (src/), Python (impl/python/), JavaScript/TypeScript (impl/js/) -- all passing the corpus and cross-checked to project identically. Corpus: 11 valid + 5 invalid vectors. Next: Go (CSON-8), a printer (CSON-9), multi-impl CI (CSON-10).

A cross-implementation checker that SKIPS a missing toolchain silently narrows its own coverage. Locally that is right; in CI a failed Go install would make the check pass while comparing nothing. cross-check.mjs now takes CSON_CROSSCHECK_REQUIRE, and an UNKNOWN name in it is also an error -- 'REQUIRE=rust' quietly requiring nothing is the same blind spot one level up.

Format v1.0 draft, SPEC 6 settled. FOUR implementations -- Rust (src/), Python (impl/python/), JavaScript (impl/js/), Go (impl/go/) -- all passing the corpus and cross-checked to project identically. CI (.github/workflows/conformance.yml) runs each plus the cross-check. Corpus: 11 valid + 5 invalid. Next: CSON-9 printer (unblocks CSON-6 round-trip), CSON-2 fuller corpus, CSON-3 crates.io.

A round-trip test cannot catch a bug your own parser is lenient about. The printer emitted nested-object pairs newline-separated with NO commas; every implementation here tolerates a missing comma, so print->parse passed -- but the grammar (SPEC 5) requires comma-separated pairs inside an object, and a strict parser would reject the output. Fixed, plus a test asserting the syntax directly rather than via round-trip.

decision_title: Round-trip is defined at the NODE level, not the byte level
decision_reason: The printer cannot recover comments (the parser discards them), and SPEC 2.4 makes [section] sugar equivalent to nesting, so a byte-identical round trip is impossible by construction. Defining the property as 'the projection is unchanged' keeps it meaningful and testable: values, confidence, annotations, semantic keys and version survive; comments, section sugar, key order and bare-vs-quoted key choice do not.
summary: Decision: Round-trip is defined at the NODE level, not the byte level
outcome: 11/11 vectors round-trip through the Rust printer with identical meaning in all four implementations.

decision_title: Node metadata order is FREE: confidence and annotations may interleave
decision_reason: The old grammar (node = value {confidence} {annotation}) forced confidence first. Nothing is gained by that ordering -- both are node metadata -- and it was a real trap: cson-corpus hit it and documented a 'write spec order' workaround. Three of four implementations already accepted either order; only Rust did not. Relaxing makes the majority correct and removes the trap. Purely additive: no previously-valid document changes meaning, so the format stays 1.0.
summary: Decision: Node metadata order is FREE: confidence and annotations may interleave

rejected_alternatives.option: enforce confidence-then-annotations strictly in all four parsers

outcome: A node still carries at most ONE confidence; a second is now an explicit error in all four (it used to be rejected accidentally with a misleading 'semantic key' message).

summary: The Rust parser SILENTLY CORRUPTED a document when a confidence followed an annotation.  + a following pair produced a bogus key "0.5\nb" -- the trailing-metadata loop consumed only '@', so the '~' fell through and the next pair's find(':') swallowed it. A parse that succeeds with wrong data is far worse than one that fails. Fixed by interleaving; the vector metadata_order pins it.

The Rust parser never validated the confidence range, despite SPEC 7 requiring rejection outside [0.0,1.0].  parsed and projected happily while Python, JS and Go all rejected it -- a four-way divergence the corpus was blind to because no vector covered it. Found only by testing the spec text against every implementation rather than trusting green CI.
